name: Fourth Anti-Money Laundering Directive
evidence_rating: moderate: one causal study of the beneficial ownership registers (staggered roll-out across Member States); audits and assessments of implementation; no study of money laundering itself
summary: The Directive introduced central registers of companies' beneficial owners. A study using the staggered opening of the registers across Member States finds that investment into the EU from financial havens fell once they opened, but that likely illicit owners avoided complying rather than changing behaviour (Amberger, Wilde and Wu 2025). The Commission's 2019 assessment and the European Court of Auditors (2021) found implementation uneven and insufficient, which led to the 2024 package replacing this Directive with a directly applicable Regulation from July 2027.

indicators.objective: No monitoring indicators set in the proposal; assessed through the Commission's reports listed below

literature.citation: European Commission (2019), Towards better implementation of the EU's anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism framework, COM(2019) 360
literature.title: Towards better implementation of the EU's anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism framework
literature.method: assessment (recent cases, supranational risk assessment, FIU cooperation)
literature.headline: Major divergences in the application of the framework; a structural problem for preventing misuse of the financial system; options include turning the Directive into a Regulation and an EU supervisor
literature.summary_plain: The Commission concluded that countries applied the anti-money laundering rules so differently that the system had structural gaps.

literature.citation: Amberger, H.J.; Wilde, J.H.; Wu, Y. (2025), Cross-border investment, deterrence, and compliance effects of ownership transparency, Journal of Accounting and Economics 80(2-3):101809
literature.authors: Amberger, H.J.; Wilde, J.H.; Wu, Y.
literature.title: Cross-border investment, deterrence, and compliance effects of ownership transparency
literature.method: staggered difference-in-differences exploiting the staggered adoption of EU beneficial ownership registers
literature.outcomes: cross-border investment from non-EU financial havens into the EU; compliance with registers
literature.headline: Investment from non-EU financial havens into the EU declines significantly after countries adopt ownership registers, with public scrutiny and enforcement as key drivers. Potentially illicit actors do not appear to change their investment, and instead seem less likely to comply with the registers (abstract paraphrased; effect sizes not in abstract).
literature.summary_plain: The registers required by the 4th AML Directive cut haven-routed investment into the EU, but people with the most to hide seem simply not to register.
literature.quality: causal (staggered DiD); peer-reviewed, top accounting journal

literature.citation: Collin, M.; Hollenbach, F.M.; Szakonyi, D. (2023), The end of Londongrad? The impact of beneficial ownership transparency on offshore investment in UK property, UNU-WIDER Working Paper 2023/11
literature.authors: Collin, M.; Hollenbach, F.M.; Szakonyi, D.
literature.title: The end of Londongrad? The impact of beneficial ownership transparency on offshore investment in UK property
literature.method: event-study / difference-in-differences on UK land registry purchases by offshore companies around the 2022 Register of Overseas Entities
literature.outcomes: new property purchases by tax-haven companies; compliance; prices
literature.headline: New purchases by tax-haven companies 'fell substantially' after the policy was announced and fell further once the register was set up. But GBP 44-76bn of UK property was still held by haven companies, most not yet compliant, with no strong evidence of price effects.
literature.summary_plain: When the UK forced offshore property owners to name themselves publicly, new anonymous purchases dried up, but many existing owners have not complied.
literature.quality: causal (quasi-experimental); working paper; UK post-Brexit policy, so indirect evidence for the EU register model

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2021), Special Report 13/2021: EU efforts to fight money laundering in the banking sector are fragmented and implementation is insufficient, European Court of Auditors
literature.title: Special Report 13/2021: EU efforts to fight money laundering in the banking sector are fragmented and implementation is insufficient
literature.method: performance audit of Commission, EBA and ECB; document review, sampled transposition files, survey
literature.outcomes: transposition of AMLD4; EBA breach-of-Union-law use; supervisory effectiveness
literature.headline: About a week after the June 2017 deadline only 6 Member States had declared full AMLD4 transposition, 7 partial and 15 none. Commission transposition checks took 20-40 months against a 6-month target, and the EBA made only one positive ML/TF breach finding since 2010.
literature.summary_plain: EU auditors found the 4th AML Directive was put into national law late and unevenly, and EU-level enforcement was weak.
literature.quality: descriptive audit of implementation (process, not outcomes)
literature.verified: full text read (web edition, first part)

literature.citation: European Banking Authority (2022), Opinion of the European Banking Authority on 'de-risking' (EBA/Op/2022/01) and annexed report, European Banking Authority
literature.title: Opinion of the European Banking Authority on 'de-risking' (EBA/Op/2022/01) and annexed report
literature.method: information gathered from all relevant competent authorities and external stakeholders
literature.outcomes: scale and impact of de-risking (financial exclusion) linked to AML/CFT compliance
literature.headline: Unwarranted de-risking has 'a detrimental effect' on EU objectives, including fighting financial crime and promoting financial inclusion, competition and stability, and can cause 'financial exclusion of legitimate customers'. The scale cannot be quantified for lack of comprehensive statistics.
literature.summary_plain: The EU banking regulator found that banks cutting off risky-looking customers to meet anti-money-laundering rules is excluding legitimate people and firms, though it could not measure how widespread this is.
literature.verified: press release read; annexed report not read
